t.5.11.1: Then Hanūmān, leader of the monkey troops, having nimbly crossed from the aerial palace onto the rampart, moved swiftly, like lightning amid the clouds.
t.5.11.2: Having gone all around the dwellings of Rāvaṇa without seeing Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, the monkey Hanumān spoke these words.
t.5.11.3: Laṅkā has been searched through for the most part by me as I pursue what is dear to Rāma, yet I do not see Vaidehī, Sītā, lovely in every limb.
t.5.11.4: Ponds, tanks, lakes and streams as well, rivers, the edges of marshy forests, and impassable mountains, indeed the whole earth has been ransacked, and yet I do not see Jānakī.
t.5.11.5: Sampāti, the king of vultures, declared that Sītā was here in Rāvaṇa's abode, and yet I do not see her.
t.5.11.6: Could it be that Sītā, the princess of Videha, the lady of Mithilā, the daughter of Janaka, helpless and overpowered, would submit to Rāvaṇa of wicked conduct?
t.5.11.7: I think that as the rākṣasa swiftly flew up, carrying off Sītā and fearing the arrows of Rāma, she may have fallen somewhere in between.
t.5.11.8: Or else, I think that as the noble lady was being carried off along the path frequented by the Siddhas, her heart gave way when she saw the ocean.
t.5.11.9: I think that the noble, large-eyed lady gave up her life, crushed by the force of Rāvaṇa's thighs and the squeezing of his arms.
t.5.11.10: Or surely, as he was then crossing high above the ocean, the daughter of Janaka, writhing, fell into the sea.
t.5.11.11: Alas, while guarding her own virtue, the unfortunate Sītā, friendless and alone, has been devoured by this vile Rāvaṇa.
t.5.11.12: Or else that dark-eyed, innocent lady will have been devoured by the evil-minded wives of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.5.11.13: Brooding on Rāma's face, which is like the full moon and has eyes like lotus petals, the wretched lady has passed into death.
t.5.11.14: Crying out "Alas, Rāma! Lakṣmaṇa!" and "Ah, Ayodhyā!", Maithilī Vaidehī, having lamented much, will surely have given up her body.
t.5.11.16: How could she who was born in the family of Janaka, the slender-waisted wife of Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, ever come under the power of Rāvaṇa?
t.5.11.15: Or else, I think, she has been placed in Rāvaṇa's dwelling, where she surely laments softly over and over, like a mynah bird kept in a cage.
t.5.11.17: Whether Janaka's daughter has perished, or is lost, or is dead, it is not fitting to report this to Rāma, to whom his wife is so dear.
t.5.11.18: If it is reported, there would be fault; there would be fault in not reporting it. How indeed should this be done? It seems to me a difficult predicament.
t.5.11.19: "Now that this undertaking has come to such a pass, what would be timely and fitting?" Thus Hanumān deliberated in his mind once more.
t.5.11.20: If I go from here to the city of the lord of the monkeys without having seen Sītā, what human purpose will then be mine?
t.5.11.21: This leaping of mine across the ocean will be in vain, and so too my entry into Laṅkā and my seeing of the rākṣasas.
t.5.11.22: What will Sugrīva say, or the monkeys gathered together, or those two sons of Daśaratha who have arrived at Kiṣkindhā?
t.5.11.23: But if, having gone back, I tell Kākutstha the supremely unwelcome news, 'Sītā was not seen by me,' then they will give up their lives.
t.5.11.24: Hearing the harsh, dreadful, cruel and piercing evil news concerning Sītā, which torments the senses, he will cease to live.
t.5.11.26: Hearing that his two brothers have perished, Bharata too will die; and seeing Bharata dead, Śatrughna will not live.
t.5.11.25: Seeing him fallen into distress, his mind turned toward death, the wise Lakṣmaṇa, who is so deeply devoted to him, will not survive.
t.5.11.27: Then, seeing their sons dead, the mothers will cease to live, Kausalyā and Sumitrā and Kaikeyī; of this there is no doubt.
t.5.11.29: Dejected, distressed, wretched and joyless, the unfortunate Rumā, tormented by grief for her husband, will give up her life.
t.5.11.28: Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, grateful and true to his word, will see Rāma gone to such a state, and then they will give up their lives.
t.5.11.30: Tārā too, afflicted by the sorrow born of Vālin's death and wasted with grief, will not survive when the king passes away.
t.5.11.31: With the destruction of his mother and father, and with the calamity that has befallen Sugrīva, how will even the young prince Aṅgada keep himself alive?
t.5.11.32: And the forest-dwellers, overwhelmed by grief born of the loss of their master, will beat their heads with their palms and with their fists.
t.5.11.33: The vānaras, who have been cherished by the illustrious king of the monkeys with kind words, with gifts and with honour, will give up their lives.
t.5.11.34: Never again will the elephant-like monkeys gather together and enjoy their play, neither in the forests, nor on the mountains, nor in their secluded retreats.
t.5.11.35: With their sons and wives and with their ministers, stricken by the calamity of their lord, they will gather together and fling themselves from the mountain peaks onto the rugged ground below.
t.5.11.36: The vānaras will resort to poison, or hanging, or entering into fire, or fasting unto death, or else the sword.
t.5.11.38: Therefore I shall certainly not go from here to the city of Kiṣkindhā, for I shall not be able to face Sugrīva without Maithilī.
t.5.11.37: When I have gone, I foresee terrible lamentation in the time to come, the destruction of the Ikṣvāku race, and the destruction of the forest-dwellers as well.
t.5.11.39: If I do not go back but remain here, those two righteous great chariot-warriors will keep themselves alive on hope, and so will the high-spirited monkeys.
t.5.11.41: In a land near the shore of the ocean, rich in roots, fruits and water, I shall build a pyre and enter the blazing fire, the son of the kindling-wood.
t.5.11.40: Without having seen the daughter of Janaka, I shall become a forest-dweller, self-restrained, living at the foot of trees, taking my food only with my hand or straight with my mouth.
t.5.11.42: Or, as I sit down in due form, about to fulfil myself as an ascetic, crows and beasts of prey will devour my body.
t.5.11.43: This too has been regarded by the sages as a proper way of departing from life, so I think: if I do not find Jānakī, I shall duly enter the waters.
t.5.11.44: This long night, of well-born root, auspicious and glorious with a garland of fame, has been shattered for me, who have not seen Sītā.
t.5.11.45: Or I shall become an ascetic, self-restrained, dwelling at the foot of a tree; I shall not go back from here without having seen her, the dark-eyed one.
t.5.11.46: If I return from here without having found that Sītā, Aṅgada, together with all the monkeys, will cease to be.
t.5.11.47: In death there are many evils, while one who lives attains good fortune. Therefore I shall preserve my life, for as long as one lives, reunion is certain.
t.5.11.48: Thus, bearing again and again in his mind sorrow of many kinds, the elephant among monkeys could not then reach the farther shore of his grief.
t.5.11.49: Or else I shall slay Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked one of mighty strength. Granted that Sītā has been carried off, still the deed will be repaid in kind.
t.5.11.51: Thus overcome by anxious thought, having failed to find that Sītā, the monkey, his mind gripped by brooding and grief, pondered.
t.5.11.50: Or else, lifting him up and carrying him high over the ocean, I shall offer him to Rāma, as a sacrificial beast is offered to Paśupati.
t.5.11.52: Until I see Sītā, the illustrious wife of Rāma, I will search this city of Laṅkā again and again.
t.5.11.53: And if, even on the word of Saṃpāti, I bring Rāma here, Rāghava, not seeing his wife, would burn up all the vānaras.
t.5.11.54: Right here I shall dwell, restrained in food and with my senses held in check, so that all those men and monkeys may not perish on my account.
t.5.11.55: And there is also this great Aśoka grove, full of mighty trees; I shall go into it, for it has not yet been searched by me.
t.5.11.56: Having bowed to the Vasus, the Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas, the two Aśvins and the Maruts too, I shall go forth, increasing the grief of the Rākṣasas.
t.5.11.57: Having conquered the Rākṣasas, I shall restore the queen, the delight of the Ikṣvāku race, to Rāma, just as perfection is bestowed upon an ascetic.
t.5.11.58: Having reflected for what seemed a moment, his senses tangled up in anxious thought, the mighty-armed Hanūmān, son of the Wind, rose up.
t.5.11.59: Salutation be to Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa, and to that goddess, the daughter of Janaka! Salutation be to Rudra, Indra, Yama and Anila; salutation be to the Moon, the Sun and the hosts of the Maruts!
t.5.11.60: Then Māruti, having bowed to them and to Sugrīva, and having surveyed all the directions, turned toward the Aśoka grove.
t.5.11.61: Having first gone in his mind to the lovely Aśoka grove, the monkey, son of the Wind, pondered what he should do next.
t.5.11.62: Surely, though, the Aśoka grove, dense with trees and adorned with every refinement, will be swarming with rākṣasas; it must still be looked into.
t.5.11.63: Surely guards have been appointed here and they protect the trees; even the blessed Wind, the soul of all, does not blow here with excessive turbulence.
t.5.11.64: This body of mine has been made small by me for the sake of Rāma, and because of Rāvaṇa too; but here the gods, together with the hosts of seers, will bring about my success.
t.5.11.65: May the blessed self-born Brahmā and the gods grant me success, and Agni, and Vāyu, and Puruhūta, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
t.5.11.66: Varuṇa with the noose in his hand, and likewise Soma and Āditya, the two great-souled Aśvins, and all the Maruts as well.
t.5.11.67: All beings, and he who is the lord of beings, and those others who move unseen along the path, will grant me success.
t.5.11.68: When indeed shall I see that face of the noble lady, with its prominent nose and white teeth, flawless, with its pure smile and eyes like lotus petals, lovely to behold as the clear lord of the stars?
t.5.11.69: Overpowered by force by that base and wicked one of cruel deeds, who wears a most dreadful yet ornamented garb, that helpless, pitiable woman, how indeed might she come within the path of my sight today?
